        "content": "IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON WIRELESS COMMUNICATIONS 1 Off-Grid Sparse Bayesian Learning for Direct Localization of Cyclostationary Sources with Adaptive Grid Refinement Yuexian Wang,Member, IEEE, Yiquan Zhang, Chuang Han, Ling Wang, Chintha Tellambura,Fellow, IEEE, Shahid Mumtaz,Senior Member, IEEE, Marco Di Renzo,Fellow, IEEE, and Mérouane Debbah,Fellow, IEEE Abstract—The growing number of emitters and interferences in 5G and beyond, coupled with limited array resources, poses significant challenges to high-precision passive localization. This paper addresses the off-grid direct position determination problem for cyclostationary signals in the presence of interference. We propose a sparse Bayesian learning framework that integrates cyclic cross-correlation processing with sparse array augmentation. The method constructs enhanced pseudo-snapshots by vectorizing cyclic correlation matrices and averaging entries associated with repeated difference lags, effectively expanding the virtual array aperture. An adaptive grid refinement strategy dynamically adjusts grid resolution through multi-resolution candidate generation and Newton-based optimization, while offgrid offsets are optimized via closed-form updates derived from a second-order Taylor expansion of the array manifold. A two-stage refinement procedure then corrects cyclic crosscorrelation mismatch by reconstructing and subtracting offdiagonal interference terms, leading to a purified signal model for high-accuracy estimation. Extensive simulations across overdetermined and underdetermined scenarios demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior positioning accuracy and robustness, effectively mitigating grid bias and interference while outperforming state-of-the-art counterparts. Index Terms—Cyclostationarity, direct localization, off-grid sparse Bayesian learning, interference suppression, degrees of freedom. I. W ITH the advent of 5G, wireless positioning has gained increasing attention as a key technology for next-generation communications, providing high-precision and high-resolution location services [1]. Traditional active localization, however, suffers from high power consumption, electromagnetic pollution, and poor concealment, limiting its use in cellular positioning, indoor navigation, and emergency tracking. In contrast, passive positioning, where base stations determine emitter positions solely from intercepted observations, has gained increasing attention [2], [3]. Traditional passive localization follows a two-step approach. First, the system estimates intermediate parameters from the observations, such as time of arrival (TOA) [4], time difference of arrival (TDOA) [5], direction of arrival (DOA) [6], received signal strength (RSS) [7], or frequency difference of arrival (FDOA) [8]. Second, a system of equations is formulated based on the geometric relationship between the emitters and the base stations. The emitter positions are then obtained by solving this system. Although widely used for its simplicity, the two-step strategy has inherent limitations, including error propagation, difficulty in parameter association, and inefficient information utilization. To overcome these limitations, Weiss proposed direct position determination (DPD), a single-step approach that estimates emitter positions directly from raw measurements [9]. Unlike two-step methods, DPD directly exploits the constraint that signals from the same emitter are received across multiple base stations, achieving higher accuracy [10], [11]. Antenna arrays are commonly used by dual-functional base stations to monitor the region of interest. Depending on the cooperation mode among stations, the observations can be parameterized and coherently processed using a time-domain global narrowband model, a time-domain local narrowband model, or a frequency-domain narrowband model. A global multiple signal classification (GMA) approach was proposed for DPD under the narrowband assumption [12]. Based on this model, Chenet al.formulated DPD as a multidimensional harmonic retrieval problem using nested arrays and spatiotemporal processing, increasing degrees of freedom (DOFs) and enabling the application of multidimensional spectrum estimation techniques [13]. Subsequently, they solved the DPD problem using sparse Bayesian learning without requiring prior knowledge of the number of emitters [14]. For the time-domain local narrowband model, which does not require tight synchronization, several works have exploited angle and Doppler information [15]–[19]. When signal envelope variations across stations cannot be ignored due to significant timedelay differences, the frequency-domain narrowband model is employed to jointly process signals from all distributed arrays [20]–[22]. Most existing work focuses on localizing emitters with unknown and arbitrary waveforms, without leveraging waveform properties. In fact, exploiting such prior information can further improve localization performance. For example, BarShalom and Weiss investigated DPD for orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) signals in multipath environments, developing an ML estimator that exploits both unknown data tones and known pilot tones to outperform general DPD [23], [24]. Subsequent works extended OFDM-based DPD to incorporate time-of-arrival, direction-of-arrival, and Doppler shift [25], [26]. Noncircular signals, another widely used communication signal class, have also been exploited for DPD by leveraging virtual array aperture expansion and increased degrees of freedom [27]–[29]. Oispuu and Nickel studied intermittent emission scenarios using minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR)- and maximum likelihood (ML)type DPD methods [30]. To overcome their sensitivity to missing emissions, Hao and Wan later employedK-means clustering to adaptively identify active sources, decoupling the problem into independent single-source localizations [31]. Cyclostationary signals, widely used in communications, are characterized by periodicity in their first and second moments. By exploiting this property, Reuven and Weiss developed the cyclic direct position determination (CDPD) algorithm, which processes signals of interest (SOIs) while effectively suppressing noise and strong interference [32]. Numerous high-resolution DPD methods have also been proposed. Wang used multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithms to study the effect of target-receiver geometry on localization performance [33]. The weighted-MUSIC DPD method was extended to self-localization networks in [34]. Wuet al.proposed a DPD self-calibration method for single moving arrays under insufficient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) or snapshot number [35]. Haoet al.investigated direct ML position determination for dense emitters under finite observation resources [36], while Wanget al.applied importance sampling combined with ML to DPD for multiple stationary targets with moving sensor arrays [37]. When the number of sources is unknown, MUSIC and ML methods fail, and MVDR-based approaches can be used [31], [38], [39]. Compared with traditional DPD methods, sparse signal representation offers higher accuracy and robustness, particularly under challenging conditions such as limited snapshots, low SNR, and few base stations. Among sparse recovery approaches,l 0-norm-based methods have been successfully applied to DPD. A direct localization method robust to partial gain-phase errors was proposed in [40] using reweighted smoothed sparse reconstruction. Yanet al.introduced a weightedl 0-norm DPD algorithm for a single mobile base station with an extended nested array [41]. Jinet al.proposed SaDPD, a structure-aware method combining row-element sparsity and low-rank constraints with ADMM optimization for sub-meter indoor localization [42]. Sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) avoids the difficulty of choosing regularization parameters. Chenet al.developed a positioning model within an SBL framework using DOA and TDOA-DOA measurements, achieving higher accuracy than traditional methods [14]. Subsequently, an off-grid DPD algorithm based on SBL was proposed in [43], and a block SBL framework was applied to DPD in [44]. Recently, Liet al.developed an off-grid DPD algorithm for noncircular signals with a grid refinement strategy to reduce computational complexity [45]. While this method improves accuracy over circular-signalbased approaches, it requires prior knowledge of the noncircular phase, a condition that is often difficult to satisfy in practice. This paper addresses the problem of localizing multiple emitters in the presence of cyclostationary signals and interferences with different cyclic frequencies. We propose an off-grid direct localization technique within a sparse Bayesian learning framework that combines cyclostationary processing with sparse arrays. The method constructs pseudo-snapshots from vectorized cyclic covariance matrices after redundancy averaging over identical difference lags, imposes a Laplacian prior to exploit joint sparsity, and incorporates a second-order Taylor approximation for off-grid correction. An iterative inference scheme updates posterior statistics and position offsets, and the final emitter positions are determined by identifying peaks in the posterior mean spectrum. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: •We propose a systematic direct localization framework that integrates cyclic cross-correlation processing with sparse array augmentation. By constructing enhanced pseudo-snapshots from vectorized cyclic correlation matrices and coherently averaging repeated differencecoarray entries, the method exploits the inherent structure of cyclostationary signals to synthesize a virtual array with an expanded aperture. This approach not only increases the available DOFs but also establishes the foundation for high-resolution, off-grid position estimation in underdetermined scenarios. •We formulate the off-grid direct localization problem under a hierarchical sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework. A Laplacian prior is employed to promote joint spatial sparsity across the SOIs. Crucially, we derive closed-form update rules for the off-grid offsets via evidence maximization (Type-II ML), which are optimized iteratively within the Bayesian inference loop to eliminate discretization errors inherent to fixed-grid methods. •We introduce an adaptive grid refinement strategy to overcome the limitations of predefined discrete sampling. This strategy dynamically adjusts the grid resolution by generating multi-resolution candidates in polar coordinates around high-probability locations and selecting the optimal one by maximizing a local objective function using Newton’s method. CONCLUSION This paper addresses the off-grid DPD problem for cyclostationary signals in the presence of interference using an SBL framework that integrates cyclic cross-correlation processing with sparse array augmentation. The core innovations include pseudo-snapshot construction via vectorized cyclic correlation matrices and redundancy averaging over repeated difference lags for virtual aperture expansion, a two-stage refinement that corrects cyclic cross-correlation mismatch, closed-form off-grid offset updates via a second-order Taylor expansion, and adaptive grid refinement with multi-resolution candidate generation and Newton-based optimization. Simulation results across overdetermined and underdetermined scenarios demonstrate superior localization accuracy and robustness, effectively mitigating grid bias and interference.
